findings.headline: Large under-borrowed position (£280m) cannot continue indefinitely; external borrowing at high rates will eventually become necessary
findings.detail: Council's Capital Financing Requirement is £800.068m but gross borrowing only £519.963m — a gap of £280.105m. This is covered by internal reserves and cash. The council presents this as prudent (saving £5.667m/year in net interest costs versus external borrowing). However, this strategy is not sustainable long-term; reserves are finite and will eventually be depleted.
findings.matters: Illustrates that council's stated interest-rate benefit from under-borrowing is dependent on continued access to internal cash. Once reserves are drawn down, council must borrow externally. If that happens when rates are high (as now), debt service costs will rise sharply and compress revenue flexibility.
findings.figures: CFR £800.068m; Gross borrowing £519.963m; Under-borrowed position £280.105m; stated annual interest saving £5.667m at 2025/26 rates
findings.quote: To illustrate the benefit of having an under borrowed position: if the Council was to externally borrow £280.105m (over 25 years at the PWLB rate on 01/04/2025 of 6.15%), this would result in external annual interest costs in the order of £17.226m. The interest foregone on the use of internal funds would be £11.559m (based on current average interest rate of 4.13% for 2025/26). This produces a net benefit of £5.667m.

findings.headline: CCLA property fund showing £2.976m unrealised loss; council will absorb loss from General Fund if market does not recover and IFRS9 override expires
findings.detail: Council holds £20m in a CCLA pooled property fund, currently valued at £17.024m. The loss is held in an unusable reserve under IFRS9 statutory override (currently to 31 March 2029). If the property market does not recover to purchase price and the override is not extended, the council must cover the gap from its General Fund revenue.
findings.matters: Potential future charge to revenue budget; represents financial risk to council's flexibility if property values do not recover over the next 3 years. Also a signal that property-backed investments are under pressure.
findings.figures: £20m invested; £17.024m current valuation; £2.976m unrealised loss; override expires 31/03/2029
findings.quote: If the market does not recover sufficiently to bring the value of the fund up to the purchase price and the statutory override is not extended the council will need to meet any gap between price and valuation from the General Fund.

findings.headline: Interest rate environment has deteriorated markedly; Middle East conflict driving inflation and PWLB rate rises into late 2026 and 2027
findings.detail: The report explicitly links the Middle East conflict to upward pressure on energy costs and inflation. Inflation expected to exceed 4% in 2026/27; PWLB rates rose materially in March 2026 and the Bank of England signalled readiness to raise rates if inflation picks up. The 25-year PWLB rate closed at 6.29% on 31/03/2026, up from 5.78% low earlier in the year.
findings.matters: Future borrowing will be significantly more expensive. Council's temporary loans must be refinanced at higher rates. Any capital programme expansion is now costlier. Debt service costs will rise as existing borrowing matures and is refinanced.
findings.figures: Oil $100/barrel (50% higher than pre-conflict); inflation forecast >4%; PWLB 25-year rate 6.29% at year end; Bank Rate at 3.75%, forecast to potentially rise to 4.0–4.25%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, latest information indicates UK inflation is likely to increase to over 4% in the coming months as oil prices, for example, remain close to $100 per barrel, over 50% higher than before the Middle East conflict started.

findings.headline: Council deliberately exceeded historic maturity structure limits to access cheaper short-term inter-authority market rates
findings.detail: The under-12-months borrowing category briefly exceeded the council's historical authorised limit (of 25%) to maximise use of short-term inter-LA markets where rates were "significantly more favourable" than long-term PWLB. The council notes it will review limits in 2026/27 for "greater flexibility to respond to the current volatile economic environment."
findings.matters: Shows the council prioritising short-term tactical rate savings over prudential stability; borrowing more heavily in maturities under one year creates refinancing concentration risk, exactly the risk that is crystallising now as these loans come due.
findings.figures: Under 12 months actual £155m vs historical limit range 0–25%; PWLB rates 1-year 4.52% average vs long-term 5.38–6.06%
findings.quote: Under 12 months category was over the Council's historic authorised limit for a short period of time. To ensure we maximised the benefit from use of short term inter LA markets where rates were significantly more favourable compared to long term PWLB rates. Limits will be reviewed in 2026/27 to allow for greater flexibility to respond to the current volatile economic environment.

findings.headline: £100m of temporary inter-authority loans mature between May 2026 and January 2027, requiring refinancing in a rising-rate environment
findings.detail: Wiltshire has £100m of short-term borrowing from other councils and combined authorities, taken at 4.55%–5.5%, with maturity dates ranging from 29 May 2026 to 8 January 2027. This needs refinancing imminently, and current PWLB rates have risen sharply — the 25-year rate reached 6.29% in late March 2026.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk in a deteriorating rate environment; if rates continue rising due to inflation concerns, council will face significantly higher borrowing costs when these mature. The Middle East conflict and inflation spike above 4% make rates likely to stay elevated.
findings.figures: £100m total; individual loans £5m–£30m at 4.55%–5.5%; PWLB 25-year rate at 31/03/2026 was 6.29%
findings.quote: Temporary (Cashflow) Loans - Lender Start Date Maturity Date Amount £m Rate % [detailed in Table 17]

findings.headline: Council shifted to temporary borrowing at 4.55%–5.5% to fund DSG/High Needs Block deficit instead of planned longer-term borrowing
findings.detail: The council's budget had assumed longer-term borrowing, but operational need to fund the Dedicated Schools Grant/High Needs Block deficit forced it to use temporary inter-authority borrowing at materially higher rates while awaiting government funding decisions. Temporary rates of 4.55%–5.5% were cheaper than long-term PWLB rates at the time, but this is a tactical response to a structural deficit.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a systemic problem across councils in England; councils are either running deficits or drawing reserves against them. Wiltshire's willingness to borrow at high short-term rates to manage it signals the deficit is real and ongoing, not a one-year blip.
findings.figures: £100m temporary borrowing at 4.55%–5.5% maturity; original budget assumption was 4.10%
findings.quote: the operational needs (Funding the DSG/High Needs Block deficit) required great shorter-term debt then previously forecasted. Temporary borrowing was cheaper then longer-term borrowing, especially as the council was awaiting to understand the government's funding proposals for DSG

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update July 2026 (final)
findings.headline: Audit recommendations raised in 2018/19 have not been fully addressed seven years later
findings.detail: When Grant Thornton followed up recommendations from the 2018/19 audit during 2024/25, they 'were unable to fully conclude that these had been addressed.' This multi-year failure to resolve audit findings indicates either insufficient management capacity or lack of prioritisation of financial control improvement.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit recommendations over seven years suggest the council lacks either the capability or commitment to remediate control weaknesses—a pattern that undermines confidence in management's ability to manage financial risk
findings.figures: 2018/19 recommendations (now seven years old); follow-up work in 2024/25
findings.quote: A number of recommendations were raised as part of the 2018/19 disclaimed audit. We followed these up as part of our 2024/25 audit and were unable to fully conclude that these had been addressed.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update July 2026 (final)
findings.headline: Auditors explicitly do not expect to issue an unqualified audit opinion on 2025/26 accounts despite dedicated assurance rebuilding
findings.detail: Despite having an agreed rebuild plan and receiving government grant funding (£131,619 council, £26,948 pension fund) to restore assurance, Grant Thornton states: 'we do not expect to be able to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements in advance of the backstop date.' The rebuilding effort is planned to span multiple years.
findings.matters: The auditor's explicit statement that they cannot achieve an unqualified opinion even after focused rebuild work signals fundamental financial control problems that will persist—a severe constraint on the council's financial credibility and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: £131,619 council grant, £26,948 pension fund grant; rebuild commencing August 2026
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion issued for the previous 6 financial years, and a lack of assurance over in year transactions and closing balances for the previous audit year we do not expect to be able to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements in advance of the backstop date.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update July 2026 (final)
findings.headline: 2024/25 accounts were delivered significantly after deadline; initial audit revealed unreconciled cash balances and account reconciliation issues
findings.detail: Draft 2024/25 accounts were provided 5 September 2025 and full accounts (with group accounts) on 7 October 2025—significantly past the statutory deadline, resulting in a formal statutory recommendation. When auditors began testing, they identified unreconciled cash balances and issues reconciling account balances, preventing planned audit progress.
findings.matters: Late accounts delivery signals weak financial control discipline; unreconciled cash and account balances indicate either poor controls over cash management or the potential for material undetected error in reported numbers
findings.figures: Draft accounts 5 September 2025; full accounts 7 October 2025; both described as 'significantly after the deadline'
findings.quote: The Accounts for 2024/25 were delayed in being presented for audit with the original draft, which did not include the Group Accounts, being provided to us on 5 September 2025 and subsequently, the full version of the accounts which included the Group Accounts were provided to us on 7 October 2025. This was significantly after the deadline and resulted in a statutory recommendation being raised. Initial audit testing in 2024/25 revealed issues reconciling account balances and unreconciled cash balances.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update July 2026 (final)
findings.headline: No assurance exists over 2025/26 opening balances or closing reserves position due to prior year disclaimers
findings.detail: As a direct consequence of six years of disclaimed opinions, Grant Thornton states they have no assurance over the council's 2025/26 opening balances and no assurance over the closing reserves balance due to uncertainty over the opening amount. This eliminates the auditor's ability to verify a fundamental financial position metric.
findings.matters: Unknown opening balances and reserves mean the council cannot demonstrate what reserves it actually holds or what is available to cover spending—critical for any lending decision and for the s151 officer managing cash
findings.figures: Zero assurance over opening balances and reserves for 2025/26 audit year
findings.quote: As a result, for 2025/26: • we have no assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and • no assurance over the closing reserves balance also due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.paper_title: Wiltshire Council and Pension Fund Audit progress report and sector update July 2026 (final)
findings.headline: Wiltshire has received disclaimed audit opinions for six consecutive years (2020/21 to 2024/25) and no full audit has been completed since 2018/19
findings.detail: The council's accounts have been disclaimed under the statutory backstop for all years from 2020/21 through 2024/25. The prior 2018/19 opinion was qualified and 2019/20 was disclaimed due to weak control environment. Grant Thornton was appointed for year ended 31 March 2024 and has no assurance over the 2023/24 opening balances. Significant issues identified in 2018/19 remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Six consecutive years without an audit opinion means lenders and stakeholders have no independent verification of the council's financial position, reserves, or true borrowing capacity—the core information needed to assess lending risk
findings.figures: Six consecutive disclaimed years (2020/21–2024/25); one full audit since 2018/19
findings.quote: For the years 2020/21 to 2024/25 the authority audit opinions were disclaimed under the backstop. The 2018/19 opinion was qualified and 2019/20 was disclaimed to a weak control environment. We were appointed your auditor for the year ended 31 March 2024 and the impact of these disclaimed audit reports has been no assurance over your 2023/24 opening balances. A full audit has not been completed since this date.

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Investment in CCLA Property Fund at unrealised loss, with regulatory cliff-edge risk in 2029
findings.detail: The council holds a long-term investment in the CCLA Property Fund. The capital growth has not been sufficient to reach the price paid, contrary to expectation. A change in accounting regulation now requires losses to be recognised, but government provided a statutory override until 31 March 2029. The council set aside £2.5m from treasury gains this year to mitigate future risk.
findings.matters: The override expires in 2029 and the council will then have to recognise the difference between price paid and current value. This is a contingent liability that could pressure reserves in three years.
findings.figures: £2.5m set aside from 2025/26 gains; regulatory override ends 31 March 2029
findings.quote: At this stage the capital growth has not been sufficient to reach the price paid, as was expected... Government have provided a statutory over-ride to support the change in regulation so that losses do not need to be recognised for existing investments but this over-ride is due to end on 31 March 2029 at which point the council will need to recognise the difference between price paid and value of the investment. £2.5m is being set aside from the gains in treasury management activity this year to support the risk for the council in future years

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Savings delivery missed by £2.292m (14.92% of target), with unachieved savings flowing into next year's budget gaps
findings.detail: The council targeted £15.365m savings for 2025/26 and delivered £13.073m (85.08%). £2.292m of planned savings were not achieved. The paper notes 'The delivery of savings remains a focus for the Council' and that undelivered savings 'will have a direct impact on the scale of savings to be delivered in future years'.
findings.matters: Missing 15% of planned savings suggests either over-optimistic targeting or delivery challenges. If the council cannot achieve planned savings in year, it reduces confidence in forward projections.
findings.figures: Targeted savings £15.365m; delivered £13.073m (85.08%); unachieved £2.292m (14.92%)
findings.quote: At outturn 2025/26 of the £15.365m savings targets £13.073m (85.08%) is assessed as having been fully delivered. This leaves a net £2.292m (14.92%) as not achieved

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: S151 Finance Officer role marked as 'Interim', signalling transition in finance leadership
findings.detail: The document is signed by 'Andrew Hardingham, Interim Chief Finance Officer (S151)' with Sarah Higgins as 'Director - Finance (Deputy S151 Officer)'. The word 'Interim' indicates the statutory chief finance officer post is not permanently filled, creating uncertainty around financial continuity.
findings.matters: An interim S151 officer may signal recent departure, planned transition, or maternity/absence cover. This matters to lenders assessing financial management stability and decision-making continuity.
findings.figures: S151 role status: Interim as of 25 June 2026
findings.quote: Andrew Hardingham, Interim Chief Finance Officer (S151)

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reaching £104.8m, with council facing £14.5m liability after government write-off
findings.detail: High Needs block overspent by £20.757m in 2025/26. EHCP numbers grew 8% to 7,080 learners. The government announced a 90% write-off of deficits accrued to 31 March 2026 (expected ~£90.3m), BUT the council will still owe £14.503m. Additionally, the council 'is expected to be required to fund an element of the deficits arising in the 2026/27 and 2027/28 financial years which could be in the region of £149.521m'.
findings.matters: Even with government support, the council faces a £14.5m liability from DSG deficit and potential £149.5m exposure over two more years. This is a structural imbalance in how special needs are funded nationally versus locally.
findings.figures: High Needs overspend £20.757m; cumulative DSG deficit £104.829m; expected government write-off ~£90.3m; council residual liability £14.503m; forecast future exposure ~£149.521m
findings.quote: It is expected that the council will be required to fund an element of the deficits arising in the 2026/27 and 2027/28 financial years which could be in the region of £149.521m. With the expected High Needs Stability Grant it is forecast that the council will need to fund £14.503m up to 31 March 2026 and £14.952m for the deficit accrued over the following two years

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Children in residential care overshooting budget by £4.4m due to placement market shortage and complexity
findings.detail: Independent fostering agency care runs £192/week higher than the £896 budgeted. External residential care costs £2,200/week above the £3,800 budget. The council had budgeted 453 children in care but held 491 by year end (above their 407-469 target range). The paper calls this 'a significant impact on our budgetary overspend'.
findings.matters: A national placement sufficiency crisis is driving up unit costs faster than forecast. The council is building in-house capacity (3 homes secured, 1 with Ofsted approval, 3 young people placed so far) but this is years away from full impact.
findings.figures: External residential care £4.4m overspend; children in care 491 vs budget 453; IFA prices £896+£192/week; residential £3,800+£2,200/week
findings.quote: The challenging marketplace and complex needs of young people has led to an overspend of £4.4m external residential care... The average weekly price of independent fostering agency care is £192 higher than the £896 budgeted. The average weekly price of external residential care is £2,200 higher than the £3,800 budgeted

findings.paper_title: Year End Revenue Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspending by £5.627m driven by higher-need placements and care cost inflation
findings.detail: Young people transitioning to adult care cost £1.721m against a budget of £0.896m. Care providers secured £3.107m in cost uplifts due to National Insurance and wage pressures, plus £1.675m in unbudgeted spot contract uplifts. The council explicitly identifies these as ongoing pressures and has built £8.550m into 2026/27 to manage them.
findings.matters: Demand-led social care is growing faster than planned and consuming increasing budget share annually. The council signals this will persist as a structural pressure.
findings.figures: Adult Services £5.627m overspend; young people transition £1.721m actual vs £0.896m budgeted; provider uplifts £3.107m + £1.675m; £8.550m carried forward as pressure
findings.quote: We are seeing however that those we are supporting have more complex needs... The cost of care to support these individuals is therefore greater and has led to an increase in spend. These pressures are on-going and £8.550m was built into the budget for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: External grant funding reduces council borrowing need but creates delivery pipeline risk
findings.detail: DfE High Needs grant of £7.726m received in 2025/26 used to reduce borrowing. Up to £14.701m from Homes England's Social and Affordable Homes Programme 2026-2036 approved but only £1.2m confirmed to date. Reliance on phased grant confirmations creates forecast uncertainty.
findings.matters: While reducing near-term borrowing need, phased grant confirmations and unconfirmed funding create uncertainty in capital planning and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £7.726m High Needs grant confirmed; £14.701m Homes England grant approved (£1.2m confirmed)
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the council received confirmation of £7.726m of High Needs Place Allocation from the DfE. Cabinet is now asked to approve that this sum is used to reduce the remaining borrowing on the High Needs Capital Scheme line. At this stage £1.2m of the anticipated grant total has been confirmed. Cabinet is asked to approve that this grant is accepted and used to offset borrowing against the Council House Build Programme Capital Scheme line over future years.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge of £24.393m set for 2026/27, creating £24.4m annual revenue obligation from capital spend
findings.detail: The final borrowing figure for 2025/26 capital programme sets the MRP (debt repayment charge) for 2026/27 at £24.393m. While this is £4.210m less than originally budgeted, it remains a substantial and growing revenue charge driven by historical capital borrowing.
findings.matters: MRP is a non-discretionary revenue charge that reduces spending flexibility. A £24.4m annual commitment is a significant fixed cost burden that grows with each new capital borrowing decision.
findings.figures: £24.393m MRP for 2026/27; £4.210m better than budgeted
findings.quote: The final borrowing figure for the 2025/26 capital programme sets the Minimum Revenue Provision charge for year 2026/27 at £24.393m.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Structural Maintenance and Bridges overspend of £4.354m in-year, driven by reactive pothole maintenance surge
findings.detail: Substantial overspend on Structural Maintenance and Bridges scheme in 2025/26 of £4.354m, caused by 'substantive uplift in reactive pothole filling during January and February'. This reactive spend pattern (rather than planned maintenance) suggests deteriorating road condition or deferred maintenance backlog.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance overspends indicate underlying infrastructure deterioration. Growing reactive spend crowds out preventative work and suggests rising unplanned pressures on the capital/revenue boundary.
findings.figures: £4.354m overspend; 13,746 potholes repaired; 102.37 miles of road resurfacing
findings.quote: There has been an overall forecast overspend on the Structural Maintenance and Bridges capital scheme line over the course of the year, however this has increased significantly during quarter four due to a substantive uplift in reactive pothole filling during January and February.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: 2026/27 capital programme of £259.951m acknowledged as unlikely to be deliverable in-year, signalling forecast accuracy problems
findings.detail: The combined impact of amendments results in a 2026/27 capital programme budget of £259.951m. Council explicitly states: 'It is unlikely that the council would be able to deliver a programme of this scale in year and there is an expectation that this budget will be re-profiled in part into future years.'
findings.matters: The council acknowledges its own forecasting is unreliable. A £260m programme expected to slip significantly suggests delivery capacity constraints and unrealistic profiling, which undermines budget management credibility.
findings.figures: £259.951m total 2026/27 budget; significant re-profiling expected
findings.quote: It is unlikely that the council would be able to deliver a programme of this scale in year and there is an expectation that this budget will be re-profiled in part into future years.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Stone Circle Development Company effectively dormant with only one scheme on site and nine homes expected in 2026/27
findings.detail: Stone Circle Development Company is severely limited. Only one scheme currently on site with nine homes expected to be delivered in 2026/27. The report explicitly states: 'No additional schemes are expected to be progressed or delivered.' This represents a complete halt to the development programme.
findings.matters: A council entity established to deliver housing development now delivering almost nothing raises questions about capital deployment strategy and ability to generate mixed-tenure housing. Zero pipeline suggests commercial viability issues.
findings.figures: 1 active scheme; 9 homes forecast for 2026/27; 0 additional schemes planned
findings.quote: Progress against the Stone Circle Development Company Business Plan is limited to one scheme currently on site, with nine new homes expected to be delivered in 2026/27. No additional schemes are expected to be progressed or delivered.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Stone Circle Housing Company missing acquisitions target and operating at 78.75% occupancy versus 90% target
findings.detail: Stone Circle Housing Company (council's in-house delivery vehicle with £80.491m outstanding loan balance) acquired only 85 homes against target, 15 behind. Portfolio occupancy is 78.75% vs 90% target. Void rate is 21% (worse than forecast). Q4 income £595,900 is behind budget. Arrears at £55,702.71 (average £259.08 per tenancy).
findings.matters: A council subsidiary performing below targets on yield and occupancy directly impacts revenue streams needed to service the £80m+ loan. Underperformance suggests execution risk or market demand constraints.
findings.figures: £80.491m loan balance; 85 vs target acquisitions; 78.75% vs 90% occupancy; 21% void rate; £55,702.71 arrears
findings.quote: 85 homes have completed this financial year which is 15 behind the year end target. The portfolio comprises 273 properties with 215 active tenancies (78.75%), which is below the occupancy target of 90%. This reflects the number of property completions in quarter three and quarter four which are currently undergoing refurbishment prior to letting. The void rate (stock-based) is 21%, which is worse than forecast due to the timing of completions. Quarter four income is £595,900 which is behind budget due to the delays with acquisition completions and empty homes works.

findings.paper_title: Year End Capital Investment Programme Financial Outturn Position 260625
findings.headline: Council House Build Programme slashed from 1,000 homes to 493 homes with budget cut from £294m to £130m
findings.detail: Originally planned to deliver 1,000 homes over 10 years, revised to 17 years in Feb 2025, then cut again in Feb 2026 to 493 homes (256 already completed) to align with 30-year HRA Business Plan. Budget cut from £294m to £130m, with £60.264m reallocated to refurbishment of existing stock.
findings.matters: A 50% cut in housing delivery and 56% budget reduction signals constrained financial capacity or major strategic shift. Directly impacts HRA borrowing needs and revenue trajectory, which lenders rely upon for stability.
findings.figures: 1,000 → 493 homes; £294m → £130m budget; £64m reallocated to refurbishment
findings.quote: the original budget of £294m has been reduced to £130m and £64m of this has been reallocated to the Refurbishment of Council Stock across future years. As such 493 homes are to be delivered, 256 of which are completed with the remainder to be provided by quarter two 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Stone Circle Governance - Audit and Governance Committee Biannual Report April 2026
findings.headline: Council's investment in these companies will be recovered over extended periods dependent on long-term returns and borrowing margins, creating prolonged financial exposure
findings.detail: The council's financial structure for Stone Circle companies relies on recovering its investment through a mixture of company returns and margins on borrowing issued to the companies. For the Housing Company, recovery is explicitly stated to occur over a 'significant period'. For the Development Company, recovery comes at the end of each project. This extended timeline means the council maintains substantial outstanding exposure to these investments.
findings.matters: Extended recovery periods increase the council's financial exposure and reduce flexibility if market conditions change. A lender assessing the council's overall financial position needs to understand the scale and duration of these outstanding exposures to council-owned entities.
findings.figures: Housing Company: recovery over 'significant period' through mixture of returns and borrowing margin. Development Company: recovery at end of each project plus borrowing margin.
findings.quote: The financial basis for the Stone Circle companies is predicated on loans from the Council to the company to finance their activities. In the case of the Housing company, the Council will recover its investment over a significant period through a mixture of company returns and a margin on the borrowing issued.

findings.paper_title: Stone Circle Governance - Audit and Governance Committee Biannual Report April 2026
findings.headline: Stone Circle Housing Company shifting business model to acquire Registered Social Landlord and target Key Workers at 80% of market rent, signalling move away from original affordability rationale
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Business Plan pivots from the original model of renting between Local Housing Allowance and market rates to a new focus on Key Workers at 80% of market rent. The company is also investigating acquisition of an existing Registered Social Landlord rather than pursuing independent registration, a significant structural change intended to access government grants.
findings.matters: Mid-course changes to the fundamental business model of council-backed investments suggest either market-driven adjustment or that the original financial assumptions are not delivering as planned, affecting the council's return on investment.
findings.figures: Revised rental target: 80% of market rent for Key Workers in 1 and 2 bedroom flats. Current portfolio: 268 properties with 9 units due to complete shortly.
findings.quote: A Business Plan 2026/27 was agreed that sought to focus rental to Key Workers at 80% of market rent in 1 and 2 bedroom flats. The other significant change has been the decision for Stone Circle to investigate acquiring a Registered Social Landlord (rather than to pursue registration itself).

findings.paper_title: Stone Circle Governance - Audit and Governance Committee Biannual Report April 2026
findings.headline: Council commissioned external commercial review of Housing Company in January 2026, indicating governance or operational concerns required specialist assessment
findings.detail: The Shareholder Group explicitly requested an external review of the Housing Company and alternative operational models. RedQuadrant consultancy was commissioned to provide recommendations, which were considered in March 2026. The commissioning of specialist external review suggests the council identified gaps in internal governance or operational capacity.
findings.matters: The need for external commercial review may signal governance, operational, or strategic concerns within the council's management of these companies, which could indicate management capacity constraints.
findings.figures: Review commissioned 20 January 2026; RedQuadrant reported 17 March 2026.
findings.quote: On 20 January 2026 the Shareholder Group asked for: 'An external review of the Stone Circle Housing Company, the current model and seek advice in relation to other available models, for consideration by the Shareholder Group at its next meeting in March 2026.'

findings.paper_title: Stone Circle Governance - Audit and Governance Committee Biannual Report April 2026
findings.headline: Stone Circle Development Company shows limited momentum with only one active project; council acknowledges overall loss if no additional developments proceed
findings.detail: The Development Company is currently focused solely on Priestley Grove, Calne (9 units), scheduled for completion in 2026. The Shareholder Group has identified no additional land opportunities for the company. The council's own financial assessment explicitly states that if this remains the only completed project, the company will generate an overall loss that will be absorbed slowly through rental income on retained properties.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's capital deployment through this company is generating planned returns or whether the council faces hidden losses on its investment that could affect future financial capacity.
findings.figures: Priestley Grove: 9 units under construction, scheduled completion 2026. No additional development sites identified.
findings.quote: If the Priestly Grove project remains the only site completed the overall loss will be mitigated over time through rental income.

findings.headline: New borrowing will incur revenue costs from cost of carry as borrowing rates exceed investment returns
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that when it borrows in advance of spending, the temporary cash surplus generates investment returns lower than the borrowing cost. With planned borrowing of £137.247m in 2026/27 against a capital programme running below historical delivery, this gap will create a net cost to the revenue budget.
findings.matters: This represents a structural cost embedded in the treasury strategy that must be absorbed by operating budgets. Combined with the capital programme delivery risk above, cost of carry could become material to the council's outturn.
findings.figures: Planned borrowing 2026/27: £137.247m; budgeted investment returns 3.60% vs PWLB certainty rate at gilts+80bps
findings.quote: there will be a cost of carry (the difference between higher borrowing costs and lower investment returns), to any new short or medium term borrowing that causes a temporary increase in cash balances, and this position will, most likely, incur a revenue cost.

findings.headline: Loans to council-owned Stone Circle company require impairment provisions due to repayment uncertainty
findings.detail: The council has lent £75.299m cumulatively to its wholly-owned commercial company Stone Circle. Paragraph 37 states the council is applying Minimum Revenue Provision to some of this lending because the company's business plan cannot assure full repayment. This is an explicit acknowledgment that the council anticipates the loans may not be repaid in full.
findings.matters: It signals material credit risk within the council's own subsidiary that requires prudential provisions (essentially pre-funding expected losses). This could indicate cash-flow or profitability problems in the company requiring eventual write-down or additional council support.
findings.figures: Cumulative loan balance: £75.299m at 2026/27 end; in-year new lending £1.000m
findings.quote: As per the agreed policy, MRP is being applied to some of this capital expenditure, as the business plan could not give the assurance necessary that the loan would be repaid in full.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure planned to increase 49% to £212.88m in 2026/27, but acknowledged as above historical delivery
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure is jumping from £142.58m in 2025/26 to £212.88m in 2026/27. Crucially, paragraph 105 contains a direct caveat: if the council delivers at historical rates rather than this budgeted level, key indicators including the Capital Financing Requirement and under-borrowed position will be significantly overstated.
findings.matters: If capital delivery falls short as historical performance suggests it will, the council will have borrowed substantial sums that remain idle, incurring cost of carry (paying borrowing rates on funds earning lower investment returns). This creates unplanned revenue costs.
findings.quote: The capital budget for 2026/27 is higher than the value of programme that has been delivered in previous years. If programme delivery is in line with previous years, using the capital programme figures has the effect of overstating some of the estimated figures in the report, such as the Capital Financing Requirement and the under-borrowed position of the council.

findings.headline: 764 non-traditional (Reema/PRC) properties require ongoing investment to prevent escalating structural failure costs
findings.detail: The council owns 764 pre-cast reinforced concrete properties where steel corrosion can cause structural failure. A comprehensive survey is planned for 2026 of ~271 properties with budget for ~300 remedial works. The full scope and cost of remediation across all 764 is not yet known.
findings.matters: This is a known structural liability that could generate unexpected large capital demands. If failures are discovered faster than budgeted, capital programme comes under pressure. Safety risk if failures cause tenant harm.
findings.figures: 764 PRC properties in stock; 271 scheduled for survey in 2026/27; budget assumes work on ~300 properties
findings.quote: There are currently 764 PRC (Reema) properties in the housing stock. These works could have significant capital implications, as early intervention reduces the risk of escalating repair costs and potential structural failure.

findings.headline: 4.8% rent increase is essential to balance the budget; refusal creates a £1.5m immediate shortfall with no mitigation
findings.detail: The approved 4.8% rent increase (CPI + 1%) generates £1.544m in additional revenue for 2026/27. The budget does not balance without it. The council's risk commentary makes clear that rejection would force service cuts, capital cuts, or additional borrowing.
findings.matters: HRA revenue is fully dependent on government rent-setting policy. Any future cap or freeze (as happened in 2023/24) would immediately create a deficit. Government policy is a single point of risk.
findings.figures: Additional rental income from 4.8% increase: £1.544m; shortfall if not approved: £1.5m
findings.quote: The proposed 4.8% rent increase (CPI + 1% would generate C.£1.5M additional rental income in 2026/27. Refusal would create an immediate shortfall, making it impossible to set a balanced HRA budget without: Cuts to services. Reduction in the capital programme. Additional borrowing.

findings.headline: Planned maintenance budget increased £3m to £18m due to aging housing stock, with more pressures expected
findings.detail: New stock condition surveys identified significant additional maintenance works not previously budgeted. The planned refurbishment capital programme jumped to £18m for 2026/27. The council signals 'new work programmes for future years are being scoped, which may require further adjustments to the capital profiling over the coming years'—warning of more cost pressure ahead.
findings.matters: Aging housing stock is driving up capital requirement. The £18m is likely a floor, not a ceiling, suggesting ongoing cost surprises.
findings.figures: Planned refurbishment up £3m to £18m; includes 764 non-traditional (Reema) properties plus concrete balconies
findings.quote: Recent stock condition surveys have highlighted additional works that have not previously been budgeted for. The planned refurbishment capital programme for 2026/27 has increased from £15m to £18m, and new work programmes for future years are being scoped, which may require further adjustments to the capital profiling over the coming years.

findings.headline: Minimum HRA reserves of £3.615m leave the council with very limited buffer for cost overruns or income shortfalls
findings.detail: The HRA is operating at its minimum target reserve level of £3.615m, roughly 10% of annual income. This provides minimal cushion against cost inflation, tenant arrears, or unexpected capital repairs. Any significant shock would force borrowing.
findings.matters: Tight reserves amplify vulnerability to any adverse development. If rates rise further or market access tightens, this becomes a problem.
findings.figures: Opening HRA surplus £3.615m; maintained as minimum throughout plan; annual HRA income ~£38m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The HRA Business Plan ensures that revenue balances remain at a minimum of £3.6m throughout the life of the plan. The opening HRA surplus at April 2026 is projected to be £3.615m.

findings.headline: Right to Buy reform will sharply reduce capital receipts, forcing the HRA to rely more on borrowing for maintenance
findings.detail: Changes to RTB discounts (capped at £30,000 instead of £102,400) and cost floor rules are expected to drastically reduce RTB sales. This will eliminate a key funding source for the development programme and mean the HRA must borrow more or delay capital works on existing stock.
findings.matters: Capital receipts from RTB sales have historically funded new housing and major repairs. Their collapse forces a choice: borrow more (increasing debt/interest costs) or defer investment (risking compliance failures).
findings.figures: RTB discount cap reduced from £102,400 to £30,000; receipts expected to decline 'dramatically'
findings.quote: This will lead to a sharp decline in 1-4-1 receipts, meaning that the development programme needs to rely on alternative funding sources, and be scaled back accordingly.

findings.headline: Annual interest costs up £1.072m despite rent increase, as higher PWLB rates (now over 6%) outpace income growth
findings.detail: Interest payable increased by £1.072m for 2026/27 alone, reflecting both higher borrowing and elevated Public Works Loan Board rates (over 6% for long-term fixed). This cost increase offsets much of the benefit of the 4.8% rent rise and signals ongoing pressure from the external cost of borrowing.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce the HRA's ability to invest in compliance and new homes even if rents increase. This is a squeeze play: costs rise faster than revenue.
findings.figures: Interest payable up £1.072m; PWLB long-term rates over 6%
findings.quote: The interest payable budget has increased by £1.072m and is based on a projection from the new HRA Business Plan. Long-term borrowing rates remain at over 6% for PWLB.

findings.headline: Development programme cut by £76.6m net, reducing new housing delivery to 500 homes over 6 years instead of expansion
findings.detail: The council cut the development programme from £163m to £72m (gross reduction £91.646m). This was driven by affordability pressures and interest rate conditions. The programme now focuses on ~500 new homes or acquisitions over 6 years, a dramatic retreat from the previous £273m programme approved last year.
findings.matters: This signals that the HRA's core investment programme has been constrained by financial pressure rather than policy choice. It shows reduced capital generation from new assets and a defensive posture rather than expansion.
findings.figures: Programme spend reduced from £163m to £72m; net reduction £76.655m; only 500 homes over 6 years
findings.quote: Gross reduction: £91.646m (taking development spend down from £163m to £72m). Net reduction: £76.655m after accounting for lost sales receipts and grants.

findings.headline: Peak debt reduced to £318.55m but interest cover is now breached in early years, creating debt serviceability risk
findings.detail: The business plan revision cut peak debt by £122.55m (from £441.1m) through a major development programme reduction, but this left the HRA with interest cover of only 1.01x in year 1 against a 1.25x target. Interest cover is breached again in year 2 and year 7. A ratio below 1.25x signals weak debt serviceability.
findings.matters: Debt serviceability is the core concern for lenders. The HRA can no longer comfortably cover its interest costs from operations in the early years of the plan, even with a 4.8% rent increase.
findings.figures: Peak debt £318.55m (down from £441.1m); interest cover 1.01 in year 1 vs target 1.25
findings.quote: Peak debt under the latest version of the HRA Business Plan is £318.55m, compared to £441.1m in a previous iteration of the plan. Interest cover only drops below the target level ins 25/26, 26/27 and 31/32, after which the new rents improve the position.

findings.headline: School traded income at risk as schools' own funding pressures mount; this is a commercial income stream for the council
findings.detail: The council runs significant traded services to schools (e.g., support staff, curriculum services). As schools face mounting pressures from teacher pay awards and cost-of-living rises, they are likely to cut spending on traded services. The budget paper explicitly flags this: 'As funding for schools grows tighter with the teachers' pay award and other cost of living increases, the risk of income reductions rises.'
findings.matters: Commercial income streams are vulnerable in recessions or when customers (schools) face their own budget cuts. Loss of school traded income would require further savings or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: School traded income exposed to risk if schools cut budgets; no quantification of income at risk or mitigation plan provided.
findings.quote: As funding for schools grows tighter with the teachers' pay award and other cost of living increases, the risk of income reductions rises.

findings.headline: No Recovery Grant allocation from the government's £600m transitional support fund; councils on shared platforms disadvantaged
findings.detail: The government announced a Recovery Grant (£600m nationally) as transitional support to help with pressures. Wiltshire was not allocated any. The document notes this in a single line but does not address the implication. Given Wiltshire's funding settlement is already below average and its structural pressures (SEND, adults, children) are above average, missing out on this transitional pot adds pressure.
findings.matters: Discretionary transitional support typically goes to councils most in need; being excluded may indicate the government views Wiltshire's settlement as adequate relative to others.
findings.figures: Recovery Grant worth £600m nationally; Wiltshire allocation £0m.
findings.quote: The new grant funding stream announced last year (Recovery Grant, worth £600m nationally) as a transitional arrangement continues...The council was not allocated any Recovery Grant.

findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs rising 96% for 10% demand growth; adoption exits forecast to fall 20%
findings.detail: The National Audit Office has documented a 96% cost increase against 10% demand growth in children's placements nationally between 2019/20 and 2024/25. Wiltshire, as a rural authority, is more dependent on out-of-area residential provision (higher cost). The number of children exiting care via adoption is forecast to drop 20% in 2026/27, meaning children will remain in care longer at higher cumulative cost. The council has begun purchasing residential homes to manage this, but cost pressures of £1.789m demand and £1.491m inflation remain.
findings.matters: Exponential cost growth decoupled from demand growth is a definition of service breakdown. A 20% drop in adoption exits is not a local pressure—it is a national shortage of permanent placements.
findings.figures: NAO: 96% cost increase for 10% demand growth 2019/20-2024/25; forecast 20% reduction in adoption exits 2026/27; 2026/27 demand pressure £1.789m, inflation £1.491m.
findings.quote: The cost pressure of providing care has increased exponentially in the last five years. The National Audit Office confirms a 96% increase in cost for a 10% increase in demand between 2019/20 - 2024/25.

findings.headline: In-year 2025/26 overspend forecast to continue as structural pressures carry forward into 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: At Q1 2025/26, the council forecast an £8m in-year overspend driven by demand-led pressures in adults and children's social care. By Q3, 'much of the underlying pressures remain'. The budget paper explicitly states these pressures 'would therefore be likely to impact the budget position for 2026/27'. The council is managing this in-year through cost control, but if it crystallises, it 'will be met by a transfer from reserves'.
findings.matters: A council carrying forward unresolved demand pressures from one year to the next signals a break between forecasting and execution. If the Q1/Q2/Q3 position is not being closed, it will draw reserves.
findings.figures: Q1 2025/26 forecast overspend c.£8m; Q3 position 'underlying pressures remain'; if crystallised, met from General Fund Reserve.
findings.quote: Underlying pressures have been reviewed and much of the pressure being faced in 2025/26 is assessed as impacting the base budget and would therefore be likely to impact the budget position for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Core funding increase of only 0.7% is a real-terms decrease against inflation faced by the council
findings.detail: Wiltshire's overall Core Spending Power increased 4.5% for 2026/27, below the national average of 5.7%. Crucially, when removing council tax (which councils cannot control and which depends on local demographics), the government grant increase is only 0.7%—significantly below inflation. The council states this 'in effect is a real terms decrease in funding for the council'.
findings.matters: Real-terms funding cuts force a choice between raising council tax, drawing reserves, or cutting services. This council is doing all three, which suggests the settlement has genuinely eroded its financial headroom.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power increase 4.5% (vs 5.7% national average); excluding council tax, grant increase only 0.7%.
findings.quote: Excluding the elements of the council tax within the Core Spending Power the increase is only 0.7% increase which is significantly lower than the inflation increases faced by the council and in effect is a real terms decrease in funding for the council.

findings.headline: No plan to balance the budget in years 2 and 3 of the medium-term forecast; gap-closure relies on unidentified future savings
findings.detail: The council explicitly states there is no proposal to fully balance the budget across the MTFS period (2026/27 to 2028/29). While 2026/27 is balanced, the budget gap in year 2 is described as 'relatively small' and year 3 as 'only slightly more significant'. The response is to commit to 'identify changes required in service delivery' at some unspecified future point—a deferral, not a plan.
findings.matters: An unbalanced MTFS signals structural inability to match spending to resources. The council is betting on solving it later, which is acceptable only if the gap is genuinely small; the vagueness about year 3 ('only slightly more significant') suggests the council has not fully modelled the problem.
findings.figures: Budget gap years 2 and 3 explicitly unresolved; council holding £45m of savings proposals over the MTFS period.
findings.quote: there is no proposal to fully balance the budget across the MTFS period. The budget gap in the second year is relatively small and the third year only slightly more significant.

findings.headline: SEND deficit has ballooned from £1.93m to £106m in seven years with no post-2028 government solution confirmed
findings.detail: The cumulative High Needs Block deficit has grown dramatically between 2018/19 and 2025/26 forecast, driven by a 69% increase in Education Health and Care Plans against only 59% funding growth. The government extended the statutory override (allowing councils to shield SEND deficits from the main budget) until March 2028, but has not yet confirmed how councils will address the accumulated deficit after that date. A Schools Minister statement in December 2025 promised further details 'later in the Local Government Finance Settlement process'.
findings.matters: A £106m deficit that becomes the council's direct liability in three years with no confirmed remediation plan is a material structural risk. This is not a normal budget pressure—it represents government policy shifting a national problem onto individual councils.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit grown from £1.93m (2018/19) to £106m (forecast end 2025/26); 69% increase in EHCPs 2020-2025 vs 59% funding increase; spend increased 105% over same period.
findings.quote: Since 2018/19, the cumulative deficit in Wiltshire has grown from £1.93m and forecast to reach £106m at the end of this financial year.

findings.headline: Wiltshire faces a £106.9m dedicated schools grant deficit with approximately £15m unfunded after government grant covers 90%
findings.detail: The Final Local Government Finance Settlement provides approximately 90% of the cumulative DSG deficit as a grant (~£92m). However, Wiltshire's forecast DSG deficit is £106.9m, leaving approximately £15m for the council to fund from its own resources. The council has earmarked £18m in reserves to manage this exposure, but the gap represents a material reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: A £15m unfunded deficit requires the council to use reserves, depleting a finite resource that could otherwise cover emergencies or service pressures elsewhere
findings.figures: £106.9m forecast deficit; approximately £92m government grant (90% of cumulative deficit); approximately £15m gap; £18m earmarked reserve
findings.quote: This grant will partly off-set the forecast £106.9m deficit that will leave a balance of approximately £15m for the council to fund. The council has set aside £18m in an earmarked reserve to help manage the risk of this deficit.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care £2m saving assumes successful renegotiation of spot contracts and provider rates
findings.detail: Savings depend on 'reviewing commissioning approaches in Adult Social Care and reducing need for spot provision' and 'negotiating alternative contractual arrangements'. No detail on whether providers will accept lower rates or whether volume of need will increase.
findings.matters: ASC demand is typically rising and providers' cost bases are fixed. Assumed savings may not materialise if demand increases or providers resist rate cuts.
findings.figures: £2m saving in 2026/27
findings.quote: By managing costs and negotiating alternative contractual arrangements, we can maintain quality care, reduce unnecessary spending and create a more stable financial footing for future years. An additional £2m saving can be achieved in 2026/27 in this area.

findings.headline: SEND and Adult Social Care demand pressures remain highest risk despite savings proposals
findings.detail: The council's own risk register identifies 'inability to meet increasing demand for EHCPs and support to children with SEND within available budgets' and 'inability to provide sufficient social care placements to meet demand within available budgets' as the two highest-concern strategic risks. The alternative budget does not address root causes of rising demand.
findings.matters: These are statutory obligations. Unmet demand creates service failure risk and potential legal challenge.
findings.figures: Listed as highest concern in risk assessment; Adult Social Care £2m savings proposed but demand is rising
findings.quote: Of these, the inability to meet increasing demand for EHCPs and support to children with SEND within available budgets, and the inability to provide sufficient social care placements to meet demand within available budgets are of highest concern based on current risk assessments.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve adequacy assessment not yet updated for increased savings burden
findings.detail: The S151 officer states the risk assessment for reserves adequacy 'has not been updated with the increased total value of savings due to the scale and pace of work being undertaken'. This will be done before committee meets, but means current reserve levels may not reflect the new savings risk.
findings.matters: Reserves adequacy is foundational to council financial resilience. Assessment lagging behind budget changes is a governance weakness.
findings.figures: £0.873m contingency reserve set aside in 2026/27; £2.5m new unspecified savings
findings.quote: The risk assessment for the General Fund Reserve has not been updated with the increased total value of savings due to the scale and pace of work being undertaken, and this will be updated before the Finance & Procurement Select Committee meet to ensure the committee are made aware of the assessment by the S151 Officer of the adequacy of reserves.

findings.headline: Melksham Bypass funding paused and reallocated; project depends on Government confirmation that is not currently forthcoming
findings.detail: £5m Melksham Bypass capital is paused because 'Government currently has no plans to progress'. £3.6m Community Infrastructure Levy is reallocated to depot development, with highways receiving £1.2m/year instead. Reintroduction depends on future Government approval.
findings.matters: Capital plan depends on external parties acting. If Government later approves the Bypass, council must find alternative funding for depots or reduce highways investment.
findings.figures: £5m Melksham Bypass funding paused; £3.71m CIL currently allocated; £3.6m CIL reallocated to depot; £1.2m/year added to highways
findings.quote: Re-profiling the capital allocation for the major Melksham Bypass highways project that the Government currently has no plans to progress is a sensible, financially responsible step. By pausing this funding and reintroducing it only if Government confirms it is ready to move forward, the council avoids tying up significant capital in a scheme that cannot yet be delivered.

findings.headline: St Stephen's Car Park: £5.1m of maintenance and demolition/rebuild spending removed; long-term covenant exposure unresolved
findings.detail: The budget removes £2.7m for maintenance/resurfacing and £2.4m for feasibility of demolition/rebuild, setting aside only £100k to 'challenge the existing covenant'. The asset's future remains uncertain and the covenant constraint is unresolved.
findings.matters: Deferred capital spend suggests the council cannot afford the work, but the covenant obligation remains. This creates future liability risk and potential forced spending.
findings.figures: £2.7m maintenance/resurfacing removed; £2.4m feasibility work removed; £0.1m set aside to challenge covenant
findings.quote: Removing the £2.7m capital allocation for maintenance and resurfacing at St Stephen's Place car park, alongside a further £2.4m budgeted for feasibility work for its later demolition and rebuilding, avoids significant unnecessary spending while the long-term future of the site remains uncertain. Instead, £100,000 will be set aside to challenge the existing covenant.

findings.headline: £15m highways borrowing removed; replaced by untested Lane Rental income and revenue funding
findings.detail: The budget removes a planned £15m highways borrowing programme and replaces it with revenue funding (£4.2m) plus Lane Rental scheme income (modelled on East Sussex). The alternative depends on new Lane Rental scheme success; borrowing avoidance saves £333k (2027/28) and £666k (2028/29) in future costs.
findings.matters: A material change to debt strategy. Reduced borrowing improves long-term affordability, but highways maintenance now depends on new, untested income source.
findings.figures: £15m borrowing removed; borrowing cost savings of £333,000 in 2027/28 and £666,000 in 2028/29; £4.2m revenue funding over 3 years; Lane Rental modelled at £2m–£4m annually based on East Sussex experience
findings.quote: By removing the plan to borrow £15m for highways spending over the next three years and instead funding it through revenue and new Lane Rental income, the council can avoid unnecessary debt and immediately reduce financial pressure. This approach eliminates borrowing costs of around £333,000 in 2027/28 year and £666,000 in 2028/29

findings.headline: £2.5m of staff savings proposed for 2026/27 with no delivery actions specified
findings.detail: The alternative budget adds £2.5m of workforce savings without documented plans. The S151 officer explicitly notes this 'increases the deliverability risk' and that the council 'has little time to take action to deliver alternative savings'. Only £0.873m contingency reserve is set aside against this risk.
findings.matters: Unquantified workforce reductions threaten service delivery and create execution risk, weakening the council's ability to meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: £2.5m staff savings for 2026/27; £7.5m additional staff savings across remainder of MTFS; £0.873m contingency reserve
findings.quote: a further £2.5m of savings has been added without specific delivery actions at this stage, which increases the deliverability risk

findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts assume bank rate will fall to 3.25% in 2027, but PWLB rates remain above long-term benchmarks
findings.detail: The council's investment earnings budget assumes rates of 3.60% in 2026/27, falling to 3.30% in 2027/28, with a long-term forecast of 3.50%. However, current PWLB certainty rates are above this 3.50% long-term forecast, creating a cost-of-carry in the near term. The strategy is explicitly cautious, reserving the right to delay borrowing if rates are expected to fall further.
findings.matters: If interest rate forecasts prove wrong and rates remain high or fall more slowly than expected, the council's debt servicing costs will be higher than budgeted, affecting revenue affordability and reserves.
findings.figures: Budgeted earnings rate 2026/27: 3.60%; 2027/28: 3.30%; long-term forecast: 3.50%
findings.quote: The current expectation forecasts bank rate to fall to a low of 3.25% in 2027... As there are so many variables at this time, caution must be exercised in respect of all interest rate forecasts.

findings.headline: Total external debt is rising sharply, forecast to reach £635.325m by end of 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's total external debt is forecast to grow from £420.664m (2024/25) to £534.132m (2025/26) to £635.325m (2026/27) — a 51% increase over three years. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), which measures underlying borrowing need, is forecast to reach £895.532m by 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in debt indicates increasing financial leverage. Lenders track debt ratios and trajectory to assess sustainability of repayment obligations and the council's ability to manage future shocks.
findings.figures: Total external debt 2024/25 actual £420.664m; 2025/26 estimate £534.132m; 2026/27 estimate £635.325m. Total CFR 2026/27 estimate £895.532m
findings.quote: Debt at 31 March 2025 £420.664m... Debt at 31 March 2026 (estimate) £534.132m... Debt at 31 March 2027 (estimate) £635.325m

findings.headline: Stone Circle commercial loans face impairment risk and are now part of MRP policy
findings.detail: The council has lent £75.299m cumulatively to Stone Circle (a wholly-owned commercial company). These loans are entirely funded by borrowing. The council has acknowledged that the Stone Circle business plan cannot give sufficient assurance the loan will be repaid in full, so MRP (a revenue charge) is now being applied to this debt. This means the council is already reserving for potential loss.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the credit risk of the council's investments. Commercial lending to a single entity, combined with the council's acknowledgment that repayment is uncertain, creates an impairment charge to revenue and represents a real financial cost to the council.
findings.quote: As per the agreed policy, MRP is being applied to some of this capital expenditure, as the business plan could not give the assurance necessary that the loan would be repaid in full.

findings.headline: Hindon Stagger project (final phase of 7-project depot strategy) faces ongoing construction and planning challenges
findings.detail: The Hindon Stagger project is the final phase of the Depot & Office Strategy. It has experienced significant challenges including its location requiring substantial additional survey work and planning approval difficulties, compounded by inflationary cost pressures. £3.722m remains in the 2026/27 budget to complete construction.
findings.matters: This is an operational infrastructure project affecting council service delivery. Ongoing delays and cost pressures on a major facilities strategy project indicate execution risk in the capital programme.
findings.figures: Remaining budget for 2026/27: £3.722m. Programme phase: final phase of seven-project Depot & Office Strategy.
findings.quote: The Hindon Stagger project is the last of seven projects that form the Depot & Office Strategy Phase 1 capital programme of works. The project has faced numerous challenges including its location requiring a significant volume of additional survey work and associated mitigations to secure planning approval for construction and inflationary cost pressures

findings.headline: Profiling of borrowing-funded schemes is critical to revenue budget; incorrect profiling creates direct revenue impact
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that the timing of capital schemes funded by borrowing directly affects revenue budget pressure. Inaccurate profiling creates volatility in Minimum Revenue Provision and interest costs within the revenue budget and medium-term financial strategy. The council commits to regular scheme reviews, but this dependency is inherent to the £274.8m borrowing programme.
findings.matters: For a lender, this signals that revenue budget stability depends on capital profiling accuracy. Slippage in borrowing-funded schemes creates unexpected revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Proposed borrowing: £274.811m over 2026/27-2032/33. Stone Circle loans (borrowing-funded): £12.040m funded by 'returns from the Stone Circle companies'.
findings.quote: If the profiling of capital schemes funded by borrowing is incorrect there will be a direct impact on the council's revenue budget. It is therefore of vital importance that schemes are reviewed regularly.

findings.headline: Major future capital requirement: car park rebuild estimated at £12m with planning costs front-loaded
findings.detail: A council-owned car park is deteriorating structurally and approaching the end of its useful life. Current essential repairs of £2.700m over two years will only extend useful life by approximately five years. The council is committing £2.400m in 2026/27-2027/28 to plan for eventual demolition and rebuild, estimated in the region of £12m. Asset covenants require replacement to maintain parking provision, making this a mandatory future investment.
findings.matters: This represents a material unfunded future capital need (£12m rebuild) that will impact the medium-term financial position. Current spending on planning signals the council acknowledges this cannot be avoided.
findings.figures: Current essential repairs: £2.700m over 2 years (£1.350m 2026/27, £1.350m 2027/28). Demolition and rebuild estimate: 'in the region of £12m'. Planning costs: £2.400m (£0.400m 2026/27, £2.000m 2027/28).
findings.quote: The car park requires a significant programme of essential repair work in order to prolong its useful life... The demolition of the structure is therefore unavoidable at some point in the coming years... With a potential demolition and rebuild cost in the region of £12m, a forecast £2.400m will be spent in preparing that programme

findings.headline: Historic capital delivery over-confidence required governance intervention to stabilise programme
findings.detail: The council acknowledges a long-standing pattern of over-confidence in programme deliverability. A Capital Investment Programme Board was established to provide challenge and validation. Spend-to-budget ratios have improved markedly from 49% (2021/22) to 85% (2024/25), indicating the governance changes are working, but the underlying issue signals historical execution risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether delivery improvements are structural or contingent on continuing governance oversight. Profiling errors affect revenue impact and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Spend-to-budget ratio: 49% (2021/22) to 85% (2024/25). Average programme spend: £100m per annum (2021/22) increasing to £177.261m (2024/25).
findings.quote: the council has historically seen over-confidence with the deliverability of the scale of the programme that has been set previously in any given year. This office[r] governance process continues to provide a robust oversight across the programme and ensures alignment with Our Wiltshire Plan priorities

findings.headline: Council's under-borrowed strategy assumes medium and longer-dated borrowing rates will fall; if rates rise or stay flat, Council faces significant 'cost of carry' losses
findings.detail: Wiltshire maintains an under-borrowed position (using reserves as internal borrowing rather than taking external loans) betting that interest rates will fall. The strategy states 'medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing higher inflation rates are addressed by the Bank of England monetary policy'. If this assumption proves wrong, the Council will have borrowed heavily at higher rates while earning lower investment returns on reserves.
findings.matters: A Council betting on falling rates faces significant interest rate risk. If rates stay elevated or rise, the 'cost of carry'—the gap between higher borrowing costs and lower investment returns—will become a material revenue drain with no policy tool to address it.
findings.figures: Forecast bank rate low: 3.25% in 2027. Budgeted investment earnings: 3.60% (2026/27), 3.30% (2027/28). Forecast investments held: £50m annually.
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent, as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing higher inflation rates are addressed by the Bank of England monetary policy.

findings.headline: Council will be £303m over its liability benchmark by 2026/27, breaching prudent borrowing limits and forcing reliance on investment reserves
findings.detail: The liability benchmark represents the prudent maximum gross debt a council should carry. Wiltshire's actual debt is projected to exceed this benchmark by £303m in 2026/27, growing to £527m over by 2028/29. This overborrowed position means the Council is maintaining higher debt than standard practice considers prudent, forcing it to hold substantial investment reserves to avoid a cash crisis.
findings.matters: Overborrowing against prudent benchmarks indicates the Council is in financial stress and relying on reserves to bridge liquidity gaps. This strategy is not sustainable long-term and signals vulnerability if reserves are drawn down.
findings.figures: (Over)/Under Liability Benchmark 2026/27: £303.168m; 2027/28: £432.026m; 2028/29: £527.031m. Forecast Investments to manage this: £50m per year from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: Years where actual loans are less than the benchmark indicate a future borrowing requirement; any years where actual loans outstanding exceed the benchmark represent an overborrowed position, which will result in excess cash requiring investment.

findings.headline: Borrowing need for 2026/27 leaps to £127.247m, 79% higher than 2025/26 forecast, requiring aggressive debt management
findings.detail: The total net financing need (external borrowing required) jumps from £71.112m forecast for 2025/26 to £127.247m for 2026/27. This sudden increase is driven by capital expenditure growing from £196.777m to £260.387m. The Council acknowledges that this capital budget 'is higher than the value of programme that has been delivered in previous years', creating execution risk.
findings.matters: A sharp year-on-year increase in borrowing need signals either accelerating capital investment (which must be sustainable) or budget overstatement. If the Council cannot spend as planned, it will have borrowed and hold undeployed cash, creating 'cost of carry' interest losses.
findings.quote: The capital budget for 2026/27 is higher than the value of programme that has been delivered in previous years. If programme delivery is in line with previous years, using the capital programme figures has the effect of overstating some of the estimated figures in the report, such as the Capital Financing Requirement and the under-borrowed position of the council.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising 79% year-on-year to £895.5m, continuing steep climb through 2028/29
findings.detail: The Council's total indebtedness, measured by CFR, is forecast to grow from £799.185m (2025/26) to £895.532m (2026/27) and reach £999.395m by 2028/29. The CFR represents historic capital expenditure not yet paid for from revenue or capital resources. The 2026/27 jump reflects both new capital spending and increasing HRA borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track the Council's absolute debt position. A £96m increase in one year—and £200m growth over three years—indicates rising financial leverage that will require increasing debt service in future years.
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). The CFR is the total historic outstanding capital expenditure which has not yet been paid for from either revenue or capital resources. It is essentially a measure of the Council's indebtedness and so its underlying borrowing need.

findings.headline: Stone Circle loans are being written off through MRP despite expectation of full repayment, signalling doubts about the commercial company's viability
findings.detail: The Council has made cumulative loans to Stone Circle of £75.299m by 2026/27, funded entirely by borrowing. The strategy applies Minimum Revenue Provision (write-off) to some of this lending because 'the business plan could not give the assurance necessary that the loan would be repaid in full'. This contradicts the stated expectation that funds will be repaid in full and indicates financial stress at the company.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the Council's subsidiary is viable. Writing off loans you expect to be repaid signals management doubt about recovery, creating direct revenue cost and reducing the Council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Stone Circle cumulative loans: £53.313m (2024/25), £74.299m (2025/26), £75.299m (2026/27); £1.000m new lending planned for 2026/27
findings.quote: MRP is being applied to some of this capital expenditure, as the business plan could not give the assurance necessary that the loan would be repaid in full.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: Future savings targets for 2026/27 will be the most significant the council has faced, but recent delivery has been uneven.
findings.detail: The council achieved £15.6m of £19.7m (79%) savings in 2024/25, with a £2.16m shortfall mainly in Adult Services. For 2025/26, the target is £15.4m with only 7.4% identified as high-risk. But auditors note that 2026/27 savings targets 'will be the most significant the Council has faced', and there is a cumulative budget gap of £5m over the medium-term financial plan period. Failure to deliver savings would force greater reliance on reserves or service cuts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the sustainability of the savings plans the council is relying on to avoid larger deficits. Recent performance shows delivery shortfalls, particularly in Adult Services, and future targets are described as unprecedented.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings achieved £15.6m of £19.7m target (79%); shortfall £2.16m; 2025/26 target £15.4m; 3-year cumulative budget gap £5m
findings.quote: Early indications are showing that savings targets for 2026/27 will be the most significant the Council has faced, and as a result, it needs to ensure that it can fully deliver identified savings targets or identify further mitigating actions in a timely way if the planned savings are not going to be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Auditors Annual Report Wiltshire Local Government 2024-25 (final)
findings.headline: The Council has revised its Safety Valve plan and now expects to reach in-year DSG balance in 2030/31, missing the original 2028/29 deadline by two years.
findings.detail: The Safety Valve Agreement was struck in March 2024 for 2023/24 to 2028/29, with the Department for Education providing £67m conditional on meeting financial targets. The Council has recognised targets were not being met and submitted a revised plan in December 2024 extending the in-year balance target to 2030/31. The DfE has not formally revised the agreement but has accepted the extension verbally. There is an ongoing risk the DfE could withdraw funding if the council continues to miss its targets.
findings.matters: The Safety Valve is the only external funding mechanism available to address the DSG deficit. If the DfE loses confidence in the council's delivery plan, funding could be withdrawn, leaving the council to cover the shortfall from its own resources.
findings.figures: Safety Valve funding £67m across 2023/24 to 2028/29; revised plan targets in-year balance by 2030/31 (two years later than original agreement)
